public_rationale: Two controlled studies of GPT-4-era models back the claim. Wu et al. (NAACL 2024) tested 11 tasks and found accuracy fell substantially and consistently on counterfactual variants that depart from familiar defaults. McCoy et al. found GPT-4 decoded a simple cipher 51% of the time when the output was common text, but only 13% when it was uncommon. That is the pattern Marcus describes: workable when a case resembles training data, fragile when it does not. Wu et al. also found nontrivial performance on the variants, which fits 'hit or miss' rather than total failure.
limitations: Reasoning models released after July 2024 are not assessed.
'Any reasoning' is broad; the studies cover selected tasks.

public_payload.normalized_proposition: Marcus says any reasoning or planning in LLMs is hit or miss: viable if a situation's particulars are close enough to the training set, but highly vulnerable if they are not.
conditions: if the particulars are close enough to the training set

statement.excerpt: Consequently, any “reasoning” or “planning” in LLMs is hit or miss, viable if the particulars of a given situation are close enough to what is in the training set, but highly vulnerable if they are not.
statement.document_title: AlphaProof, AlphaGeometry, ChatGPT, and why the future of AI is neurosymbolic

from_speaker: viable if the particulars of a given situation are close enough to what is in the training set

our_interpretation: He describes an ongoing state with no stated period. I use the GPT-4-era LLMs current at the post: from GPT-4's release (2023-03-14) to the post date (2024-07-28).
Plain reading: on controlled tests, LLM reasoning accuracy drops a lot when tasks are changed to versions that are less common in training data. It need not fall to zero.
criteria.support_condition: Controlled studies of then-current LLMs show large, consistent drops in accuracy on unfamiliar or low-probability variants of tasks they handle well in their standard forms.
criteria.contradiction_condition: Controlled studies show then-current LLMs perform about as well on novel or counterfactual variants as on familiar ones.

evidence.excerpt: Across a suite of 11 tasks, we observe nontrivial performance on the counterfactual variants, but nevertheless find that performance substantially and consistently degrades compared to the default conditions.
evidence.publisher: Wu et al., MIT/Boston University (arXiv; NAACL 2024)
evidence.explanation: Reasoning accuracy falls substantially and consistently on unfamiliar variants of the same tasks. Performance is still nontrivial, which fits 'hit or miss' rather than total failure.

evidence.excerpt: For instance, GPT-4's accuracy at decoding a simple cipher is 51% when the output is a high-probability word sequence but only 13% when it is low-probability.
evidence.explanation: GPT-4's success on a deterministic task depends heavily on how familiar the content is, which matches his claim of being viable near the training data and fragile away from it.
